pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Temperature & Thermometers (CONCEPTUAL, 0.08): temperature is how hot or cold something is; a thermometer measures it; use hot/warm/cool/cold to describe how the air feels on different days.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation (Y1 'Seasonal changes' — describing warmer/colder seasons); measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2. At 5-7, relative warm/cool language + recognising the tool. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS, ANCHOR): K-ESS2-1 (VERIFIED verbatim) names temperature among weather conditions; its assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]' — so relative hot/warm/cool/cold is exactly the target, not precise °C. DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
• Operational details — Two ideas: (1) temperature = how hot/cold, a felt property we can order (hot > warm > cool > cold); (2) a thermometer is the TOOL that measures it, and its reading goes UP when warmer, DOWN when cooler. Keep it relative/qualitative per the K-ESS2-1 boundary — the child reads 'higher = warmer' not exact degrees. Connect felt experience (a warm sunny day vs a cold frosty day) to the thermometer moving. Prerequisite: none; feeds Using Weather Instruments (7-9, reading °C) and Dressing for the Weather. Evidence: explain temperature is how hot/cold; identify a thermometer as the measuring tool; use hot/warm/cool/cold appropriately.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child explains temperature as how hot or cold something is, identifies a thermometer as the tool that measures it, and orders/uses hot–warm–cool–cold correctly for different days — relative and felt, not exact degrees.
bestPractices: Ground temperature in FELT experience first (hold something warm vs cool; a sunny vs shady spot) before introducing the instrument — the word names a sensation the child already knows.
Introduce the thermometer as a tool whose reading rises when warmer and falls when cooler; keep it relative (higher/lower) not precise °C, matching the K-ESS2-1 'warmer/cooler' boundary.
Practise ordering hot–warm–cool–cold as a scale (e.g. bath, room, fridge, freezer) so temperature is understood as a continuum, not two boxes.

Surface the classic hot/cold conflation: what FEELS cold (metal) isn't necessarily colder than what feels warm (wood) at the same temperature — at 5-7 keep this light but avoid reinforcing 'metal is always colder'.
Tie readings to weather routine: check whether today is warmer or cooler than yesterday, connecting the instrument to lived weather.
Avoid number precision and negative numbers at this age; 'warmer/cooler/about the same' is the right grain.
keyRepresentations: A large thermometer whose coloured column rises and falls, with a hot–warm–cool–cold band beside it (no fine °C scale needed).
An ordering strip: freezer → fridge → room → warm bath, placing everyday things on a hot–cold scale.
Paired 'today' scenes (sunny beach vs frosty morning) with the thermometer reading higher/lower for each.
Felt-experience cards (ice cube, warm drink, cool shade, hot sand) matched to temperature words.
commonMisconceptions: 'Hot and cold are opposite THINGS' rather than points on one temperature scale — build the continuum (warm and cool are in between).
'What feels colder IS colder' — metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature; sensation is an unreliable exact measure (that's why we use a thermometer).
'The thermometer makes/adds heat' or controls temperature — it only measures and reports it.
'Higher number = the thermometer is bigger/fuller of liquid, not hotter' — tie the rising column explicitly to warmer.
'Temperature and weather are the same thing' — temperature is one PART of the weather, alongside rain, wind, cloud.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach temperature as how hot or cold something is, that a thermometer is the tool that measures it, and the use of hot/warm/cool/cold to describe how the air feels on different days. Keep observation relative and qualitative (warmer/cooler/about the same), not exact °C. This is a design choice that stays within the K-ESS2-1 assessment boundary, which limits quantitative observations [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]. Ground the word in felt experience first, then connect that sensation to a thermometer's reading rising when warmer and falling when cooler, and build hot–warm–cool–cold as one continuous scale rather than two opposite boxes.

activities.title: Warm it up, cool it down: watch the thermometer respond
feedback: When the column climbs as the scene warms: 'The day got warmer, and the thermometer climbed up to warm — the thermometer tells us how hot it is.'
When the child orders ice, cool drink and cocoa: 'The ice is coldest and the cocoa warmest — warm and cool sit in between, all on one scale from cold to hot.'
If a child treats the thermometer as decoration: 'Watch the coloured column — it isn't just a picture, it moves to show how hot or cold it is.'
For today-vs-yesterday: 'The column is lower today, so today is cooler than yesterday.'
activities.rationale: A live cause→reading coupling lets a child see a felt change (warming/cooling) produce a moving reading, building both target ideas together: temperature is orderable, and the thermometer reports it. Keeping it to higher/lower rather than exact degrees stays within the K-ESS2-1 boundary ([curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]) and matches the KS1 qualitative grain.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 names temperature among weather conditions; assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]'; DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
DfE KS1 weather observation describes warmer/colder conditions qualitatively; measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2.
learnerActions: Start from a plain scene with a large friendly thermometer beside it whose coloured column can rise and fall against a hot–warm–cool–cold band (no fine °C scale).
Warm the scene (e.g. drag the sun high into the sky, brighten the day) and watch the thermometer's column climb up onto 'warm', then 'hot'.
Cool the scene (slide the sun behind a cloud, or move the character and the thermometer into the shade) and watch the column sink lower, toward 'cool'.
Drop everyday things onto a shelf — an ice cube, a mug of cocoa, a cool drink — and touch the thermometer to each one to see it read lower or higher for each.
Line those things up coldest to hottest, and compare 'today vs yesterday' as higher or lower on the same thermometer.
Say in words whether each change made it warmer or cooler, and how the thermometer showed it.
activities.intendedInsight: Temperature is how hot or cold something is, it can be ordered along one scale from cold to hot, and a thermometer is a tool that reports it — the reading moves up when warmer and down when cooler, so 'higher means warmer.'

activities.title: Feel first, then name it
feedback: 'Warm and cool sit in between hot and cold — that's why we can line things up from coldest to hottest.'
If a child uses only 'hot' and 'cold': 'Is it exactly hot, or more like warm? There are steps in between.'
For the freezer-to-bath strip: 'Nice ordering — the freezer is coldest and the warm bath hottest, with steps in between.'
activities.rationale: Grounding temperature in felt experience before the instrument lets the instrument name something the child already senses, and ordering everyday things builds the continuum that counters the hot/cold 'two opposite things' misconception.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 weather observation describes warmer/colder conditions qualitatively; measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2.
Classic temperature misconceptions: hot and cold treated as distinct kinds rather than a single scale, and 'what feels colder is colder' (thermal-conductivity sensation confusion).
learnerActions: Hold or look at things that are clearly warm, cool or cold (a warm drink, an ice cube, a sunny spot, cool shade) and say how each feels.
Match felt-experience cards — ice cube, warm drink, cool shade, hot sand — to the words hot, warm, cool, cold.
Order familiar places as a scale: freezer → fridge → room → warm bath, from coldest to hottest.
Decide for the air outside today whether it feels hot, warm, cool, or cold.
activities.intendedInsight: The word 'temperature' names a sensation children already know, and warm and cool are the in-between points between hot and cold — it is a continuum, not two boxes.

activities.title: Label the thermometer and compare two days
feedback: 'Right — the beach scene reads higher because it's warmer than the frosty morning.'
If a child says the thermometer makes it hot: 'The thermometer only measures and reports the temperature — it doesn't add any heat.'
If a child reads 'fuller' as 'bigger not hotter': 'No liquid gets added — the same liquid spreads up the tube when it gets warmer, so a higher column means warmer.'
activities.rationale: A clean, labelled reference consolidates the tool's parts and the relative 'higher = warmer' rule and counters the 'thermometer adds heat' and 'fuller not hotter' misconceptions. This is a static scaffold: because a key idea is that the reading MOVES with temperature, pair it with the dynamic warming/cooling activity so the rule is seen in action, not only shown statically. (The cited claim supports the relative 'higher = warmer' element; the parts-labelling and adds-heat/fuller points are standard pedagogy rather than source-specific.)
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 names temperature among weather conditions; assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]'; DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled thermometer: tap or point to the bulb, the coloured column, and the scale to learn the parts.
Open a 'higher = warmer' flap or prompt that explains which way the reading moves when it gets warmer.
Look at paired scenes — a sunny beach and a frosty morning — and say which thermometer reads higher and why.
Describe in your own words what the thermometer does: it measures and reports how hot or cold it is; it does not make heat.
activities.intendedInsight: A thermometer has parts (bulb, column, scale), it reports temperature rather than creating it, and a higher reading means warmer.

activities.title: Coldest-to-hottest ordering check
feedback: Correct ordering: 'That's the whole scale from coldest to hottest — the in-between things take the in-between places.'
If two items are swapped: 'Which of these two would feel warmer? Put the warmer one higher.'
Slider: 'Good — warmer than the fridge means above it on the scale, but you don't need an exact number.'
activities.rationale: Ordering, matching and relative-slider tasks can check the evidence targets and the continuum idea. This is a confirmation check: it verifies the scale idea but does not by itself build the cause→reading coupling, so use it after the dynamic activity.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 names temperature among weather conditions; assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]'; DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
learnerActions: Order a set of everyday things from coldest to hottest.
Match an object to the right temperature word (ice → cold, warm drink → warm, and so on).
Use a relative-position slider to set the thermometer 'warmer than the fridge' or 'cooler than a warm bath' without using exact degrees.
activities.intendedInsight: Temperature items can be placed in order along one scale, and relative language (warmer than / cooler than) describes positions on that scale.

activities.title: Warmer or cooler than yesterday? Talk it through
feedback: 'Warmer than yesterday — and you noticed the thermometer is higher today. Nice link.'
If the child only says 'hot': 'Compared with yesterday, is it warmer, cooler, or about the same?'
activities.rationale: A short spoken comparison can elicit comparative language and tie readings to the weather routine. This is an optional extension; a measurement concept at this age does not require open dialogue, so keep the prompt focused on warmer/cooler reasoning.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 weather observation describes warmer/colder conditions qualitatively; measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Is it warmer or cooler than yesterday, and how do you know?'
Give the comparison in words and the reason (how it feels, or what the thermometer shows).
Connect the thermometer reading to the daily weather routine — check today against yesterday.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparative temperature language (warmer/cooler/about the same) describes how one day differs from another, tying the instrument to lived weather.

activities.title: Same room, same temperature: feel versus measurement
feedback: When both read the same: 'They match — both sat in the same room, so both are at room temperature. The metal only FEELS colder.'

If a child predicted the metal is really colder: 'It feels colder because it pulls heat from your hand quickly — let's look at the thermometer: if both read about the same, they really are the same temperature.'
Fridge follow-up: 'Now the metal really is colder — because of where it has been, not because it's metal. Temperature depends on surroundings.'
Keep the conductivity point light at this age: name that metal feels colder without insisting 'metal is always colder.'
activities.rationale: Stating a prediction and reason before measuring, then confronting it with equal readings, targets the well-documented 'what feels colder is colder' and 'metal is always cold' misconceptions and reinforces why we trust a thermometer over touch.
sourceClaims: Classic temperature misconceptions: hot and cold treated as distinct kinds rather than a single scale, and 'what feels colder is colder' (thermal-conductivity sensation confusion).
learnerActions: Leave a metal object and a wooden or plastic object side by side in the same room for at least an hour, away from sunlight, heaters and draughts.
Feel both, then predict what a thermometer will read on each — and say your reason BEFORE measuring.

With an adult, measure both by holding the same contact thermometer probe firmly against each object until the reading stops changing (do not use an infrared thermometer on shiny metal, which can read wrongly low), then compare the readings with your prediction.
Discuss: 'If both sat in the same room all morning, could they really be different temperatures?' and 'Which do you trust more to tell you the temperature — your hand or the thermometer?'
Try the follow-up: put the metal object in the fridge and leave the wooden one out, then measure both and say what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: How something feels is not a reliable measure of its temperature: things that have sat together in the same room for long enough, away from sun and heaters, end up at about the same temperature even if the metal feels colder, because metal draws heat from your hand faster. A thermometer measures the object or air, not your sensation.

constraints: Keep observation relative and qualitative at this age — warmer/cooler/about the same, not exact °C and no negative numbers. Reading real degrees belongs to a later (7–9) weather-instruments topic.
Ground temperature in felt experience before introducing the instrument; the thermometer names a sensation the child already knows.
Build hot–warm–cool–cold as one continuous scale, not two opposite boxes.
Distinguish temperature from weather as a whole: temperature is one part of the weather, alongside rain, wind and cloud.
Handle the feel-versus-temperature point gently: acknowledge that metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature, but do not reinforce 'metal is always colder.'
The ordering/matching/slider check confirms the scale idea but does not build the cause→reading coupling; use it after the dynamic warming/cooling activity.
The labelled-thermometer reference is a static scaffold; because the core idea is that the reading moves with temperature, pair it with the dynamic activity rather than relying on it alone.
The warmer/cooler conversation is an optional extension, not a required step for a 5–7 measurement concept.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the 2D interactive as 'ideal' and claims a static image 'can't convey' the live coupling and that '3D adds nothing'; these are catalog fit rankings, not established efficacy or necessity claims. They have been softened to scoped affordances (a dynamic model makes the moving reading visible; a labelled image is a useful static reference).

Two of three sources (DfE KS1 and AAAS Project 2061 misconception research) are marked not verified/not re-fetched this session; treat the KS1 °C-at-KS2 claim and the misconception descriptions as legacy, unverified.

Conductivity note: 'metal draws heat from your hand faster, so it feels colder' mirrors the source's own assessment nextMove and is used here in qualified, qualitative child-facing feedback kept light for 5–7 — it is optional emphasis, not a required teaching point, and whether to surface conductivity at all at this age remains a judgement the source flags ('keep this light').

Activity 3 ('Label the thermometer') cites K-ESS2-1 for its relative 'higher = warmer' element; the parts-labelling and the 'thermometer adds heat'/'fuller not hotter' misconception content is standard pedagogy not directly backed by a cited source string, and no source claim was invented to cover it.

assess.poeTask: Leave a metal object and a wooden or plastic object in the same room for an hour. Ask children to feel both and predict what a thermometer will read on each, giving their reason first — most predict the metal is colder. Measuring both at the same room temperature confronts the feels-cold-equals-is-cold idea. The reason stated before measuring is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If both spoons sat in the same warm room all day, could they really be at different temperatures? Why or why not?
Which do you trust more to tell you the temperature — your hand or a thermometer? Why?
If we put the metal spoon in the fridge and leave the wooden one out, then measure both — what changes?
assess.correctAnswer: The thermometer would read the SAME temperature for both, because they have been in the same room all morning — both are at room temperature. The metal only FEELS colder to your hand; how something feels isn't a reliable way to know its temperature, which is why we use a thermometer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Touch is the true temperature — 'the metal is colder because it feels colder'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast feel with measurement: leave both in the same room, measure, find them equal; the metal just draws heat from your hand faster so it feels colder.
errorPatterns.distractor: The metal spoon really is a colder temperature, because it feels colder.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the thermometer will confirm the metal is at a lower temperature

errorPatterns.pattern: The thermometer reports how you feel — not the object's temperature
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify what the tool does: a thermometer measures the object/air, not your sensation; that's why it's more reliable than touch.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects the thermometer to agree with the hand rather than with the room

errorPatterns.pattern: Temperature is a fixed property of the material — 'metal is always cold'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same metal warms up on a radiator and cools in a fridge — its temperature depends on surroundings, not on being metal.
errorPatterns.distractor: Metal is always cold no matter where it is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says metal is cold everywhere, no matter where it has been

responseLevels.gap: Says the metal is genuinely colder because it feels colder; treats touch as the true measure.
responseLevels.full: Predicts equal readings because both sat in the same room, explains the metal only feels colder, states the thermometer (not touch) gives the reliable temperature, and transfers to the fridge case.
responseLevels.partial: Senses the thermometer matters but is unsure the readings match, or still says 'metal is just colder' while half-trusting the tool.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have both been sitting on the same table in the same room all morning. Sam touches them and says the metal one is colder, so it must be at a colder temperature. If we put a thermometer on each, what would it read, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who separates how-it-feels from measured temperature predicts equal readings. A child who trusts touch says the metal really is at a lower temperature — the well-documented feels-cold-equals-is-cold tell.
